lesson_title: The Hiking Trail: Differentiation Rules and Cubic Graphs
hook_text: Every cubic graph is a hiking trail — and the derivative is the slope under your boots. Read the whole mountain from one formula.
clip_script: A cubic graph is a hiking trail: climb, viewpoint, descent, valley floor, climb out forever. And calculus hands you the trail report before you take a step. The derivative is the slope under your boots at every point. Where is the viewpoint? Where the slope is zero — level ground. Take x cubed minus six x squared plus nine x. Differentiate with one rule — exponent falls forward, power steps down — and you get three x squared minus twelve x plus nine. Set it to zero, factorise: level ground at x equals one and x equals three. Feed those back into the original function for altitudes: a peak at height four, a valley floor at height zero. Where does the trail descend? Wherever the derivative is negative — between one and three. And halfway down, at x equals two, the path stops curving over the summit and starts curving into the valley — the inflection point, the steepest moment of the descent. One derivative, and the whole mountain is mapped: peaks, valleys, every rising and falling stretch. That is what the exam's ten-mark sketch question actually is — a trail report.
visual_style: A glowing cubic curve rendered as a mountain trail at dawn, a hiker dot moving along it, a slope dial spinning to zero at the peak and valley, altitude tags popping up, the descent stretch shading red.
pacing: Striding rhythm up the climb, a pause at each level spot, smooth run-out on the final climb.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and turn every cubic sketch into a five-step trail report.
